hops.afterHeading: The map: ranges, fibres and channels
hops.title: How rattlesnakes sense a mouse's warmth
hops.text: Rattlesnakes are often said to see infrared. The detector is not in their eyes, though, and it runs on no light-sensing chemistry. Infrared from a nearby animal warms a thin membrane stretched across a pit between each eye and nostril. In 2010, Elena Gracheva, David Julius and colleagues showed that the nerve fibres supplying that pit carry TRPA1, one of the channels in the table above. In lab recordings, western diamondback TRPA1 opened at about 27.6 °C. Versions from a boa and a python opened at about 29.6 and 32.7 °C. The snake is, in effect, feeling the mouse from across the sand.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A coiled rattlesnake on desert sand at dusk, head raised toward a small field mouse beside a cactus.
image.caption: Infrared from prey warms the pit membrane, which opens TRPA1 in the nerve fibres inside it.

hops.afterHeading: Three channels for one burn: redundancy, not a chain
hops.title: A boy who ate hot peppers without the burn
hops.text: Doctors examined one boy repeatedly from the age of three, because he ate large amounts of hot peppers with no aversion, no blotchy skin and no tears. When researchers studied him at eleven, he carried two copies of a mutation, N331K, that left his TRPV1 channel non-functional. Capsaicin on his mouth or skin did nothing. Heat still hurt, though. He detected gentle warmth as well as healthy volunteers did and still felt heat pain, at a higher threshold. Mustard oil, which opens TRPA1, gave him markedly more redness and irritation than the volunteers. Losing one channel erased the chili burn, not heat pain altogether.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A bright red chili pepper on a wooden cutting board with a small bowl of chili peppers behind it.
image.caption: With no working TRPV1, chili never burned this boy, though heat still hurt him above a higher threshold.

hops.afterHeading: A different question: where is the sensor inside the channel?
hops.title: Ground squirrels and camels with heat-dulled TRPV1
hops.text: Thirteen-lined ground squirrels and camels cope with high temperatures better than many other mammals, and in 2016 Laursen and colleagues found unusually weak heat responses in their TRPV1 channels. Capsaicin still opened both. A single amino acid swap in the channel's N-terminal ankyrin-repeat region restored strong heat responses to the squirrel and camel channels, and the reverse swap dulled heat sensitivity in rat TRPV1. Heat opening and chemical opening can therefore be pulled apart inside one protein. A residue that shifts the threshold still does not say whether that spot senses the heat or only passes it to the gate.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A striped ground squirrel standing upright beside its burrow in sunlit short grass.
image.caption: One amino acid swap restored strong heat responses to squirrel and camel TRPV1; capsaicin worked before and after.
